## MIND the Gap {#mind .tg-light .research-detail}

```{=html}
<p class="research-subtitle">A Geographic Implicit Neural Representation with Adjustable Spatial Scale</p>
<div class="research-detail-layout mind-layout">
<div class="research-copy">
<p>Geographic implicit neural representations (INRs) learn a function from coordinates to features.</p>
<p><strong>MIND</strong> produces reusable location embeddings with broad and finer spatial detail. A predictor can select the detail without retraining the encoder.</p>
<p class="research-release">Released model weights and global embeddings in Zarr on Source Cooperative.</p>
</div>
<figure class="mind-figure"><video data-autoplay controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="assets/research/mind-embedding-poster.jpg" aria-label="MIND geographic embedding globe cycling from coarse to fine-grained features"><source src="assets/research/mind-embedding.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video><figcaption>PCA colors of successive embedding chunks.<br>Compare spatial patterns; colors vary between chunks.</figcaption></figure>
</div>
<p class="research-citation">Corley et al. (2026) · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25454">Paper</a> · <a href="https://research.taylorgeospatial.org/mind/">research.taylorgeospatial.org/mind</a></p>
```

::: {.notes}
About 30 seconds.
We also work on geographic INRs, which learn functions that return features for a location.
An embedding is a set of numbers that can be reused to predict different properties of that location.
MIND learns from several existing representations and arranges its embedding into nested chunks.
Early chunks tend to describe broad geographic variation; later chunks add finer detail.
A downstream predictor can select or downweight chunks without retraining the geographic encoder.
The globe visualizes successive 64-dimensional storage chunks, each with its own PCA colors, rather than land-cover classes or change through time.
The model takes coordinates at inference; this is not a new satellite image of the selected place.
We release the model and precomputed global embeddings.
Next, PFFs ask how several existing Earth-observation products can share a compact representation over space and time.
Sources: https://research.taylorgeospatial.org/mind/ and https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25454.
:::

## Planetary Feature Fields {#pffs .tg-light .research-detail}

```{=html}
<p class="research-subtitle">Planetary Feature Fields are Scalable Earth Representations</p>
<div class="research-detail-layout pff-layout">
<div class="research-copy">
<p><strong>PFFs</strong> jointly encode satellite observations, embeddings, and map products as functions of location and time.</p>
<p>A shared neural field reconstructs each product through a small decoder.</p>
<p class="research-result">At about <strong>1,800× compression</strong>, reconstructed features retain roughly <strong>90% or more</strong> of the original downstream performance in the paper’s tests.</p>
</div>
<figure class="pff-figure">
<video data-autoplay controls muted loop playsinline preload="metadata" poster="assets/research/pff-animation-poster.jpg" aria-label="NDVI mapping demonstration comparing Microsoft Planetary Computer and Planetary Feature Fields"><source src="assets/research/pff-animation.mp4" type="video/mp4"></video>
<figcaption>NDVI access demo by Arjun Rao · original 4× animation timing.</figcaption>
</figure>
</div>
<p class="research-citation">Rao et al. (2026) · <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.37784">arXiv:2609.37784</a> · Compression relative to uncompressed source data; performance on evaluated downstream tasks.</p>
```

::: {.notes}
About 30 seconds.
PFFs learn a shared representation of several products within local regions, queried by location and time.
The clip compares NDVI mapping through Microsoft Planetary Computer and PFFs.
NDVI is a vegetation index computed from red and near-infrared values.
The animation is shown at its supplied timing and retains its original 4× label.
This access demonstration is separate from the compression and downstream-performance result at left.
The compression result is relative to uncompressed source arrays.
Downstream tests include segmentation, change detection, and classification; the percentage is relative retained performance, not absolute accuracy.
New timesteps and product decoders can be added while preserving existing outputs.
These are research results, not a claim that PFFs already distribute the FTW release shown earlier.
This leads to the evaluation question: which tasks and regions establish that a representation is useful?
Source: Rao et al., Planetary Feature Fields are Scalable Earth Representations, arXiv:2609.37784v1, abstract. Animation supplied by Isaac Corley; credit Arjun Rao, Copernicus Sentinel-2, and Microsoft Planetary Computer as shown in the clip.
:::

## Evaluating geographic models {#research .tg-light}

```{=html}
<div class="research-overview">
<div class="research-projects"><article><h3>Features of The World</h3><p>The project extends feature mapping to roads, buildings, solar panels, and trees.</p><small>Active research</small></article>
<article><h3>Benchmarks of The World</h3><p>Shared tools to compare models across tasks, sensors, and regions.</p><small>Research and evaluation tools</small></article></div>
<div class="paper"><p class="acceptance">Accepted at NeurIPS 2026</p><h3>No One Knows the State of the Art in Geospatial Foundation Models</h3>
<p>Papers use different evaluation code and methods, so reported rankings are hard to compare.</p>
<p>Performance depends on the task, sensor, and region. Strong results on selected benchmarks do not establish generalist capability.</p>
<p>We propose shared evaluation code and comparable tests across those settings.</p>
<a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12678">Corley et al. · arXiv:2605.12678</a></div>
</div>
```

::: {.notes}
About 20 seconds.
The same question applies to FTW, MIND, and PFFs: how do we know where a model is useful?
Our new methods need the same careful evaluation as the models we compare with.
Features of The World extends feature mapping beyond fields.
Benchmarks of The World develops tools for comparing model quality, geographic generalization, and compute requirements.
Our position paper was accepted at NeurIPS 2026.
Published evaluations use different code, preprocessing, adaptation methods, and scoring implementations, so reported rankings are difficult to compare.
Model performance varies across tasks, sensors, and regions.
Strong results on a few benchmarks do not establish that a model generalizes across those settings.
We propose shared evaluation code and comparable tests to make model selection better grounded.
The paper describes a community coordination problem, including our own practices, rather than blaming individual researchers.
The slide omits numerical audit results from the older preprint while revisions are in progress.
Sources: https://taylorgeospatial.org/innovation-program/features-of-the-world/ ; https://taylorgeospatial.org/innovation-program/benchmarks-of-the-world/ ; https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12678.
:::
